cases.description: PDF starter: summarize and highlight key points.

turn.prompt: Summarize this and highlight the key points

passages.text: Lecture 7 covers why some study habits produce durable memories while others fade within days.
Without review, most newly learned material is forgotten quickly: recall drops steeply in the first day and then levels off.
The aim of this lecture is to connect four techniques to the memory processes they strengthen.
Encoding turns an experience into a memory trace; deeper processing, such as explaining an idea in your own words, produces stronger traces.
Consolidation stabilizes a trace over hours to days, and much of it happens during sleep, when the hippocampus replays recent experiences.
Retrieval is the act of bringing a memory back to mind, and each successful retrieval changes the memory it accesses.
The spacing effect: reviewing material in several sessions spread over days produces better long-term recall than the same total time in one session.
Spacing works because each review happens after some forgetting, so reconstructing the memory takes effort and strengthens it more.
Cramming can raise scores on a test the next morning, but most of that gain is lost within a week.
Retrieval practice: testing yourself without looking at the answer improves later recall more than rereading the same material.
Retrieval practice works best with feedback, so that errors are corrected before they are rehearsed.
Rereading feels productive because the text becomes familiar, but this fluency is a poor guide to what you will remember.
Interleaving mixes different problem types in one session instead of practicing one type at a time.
Interleaving is harder because each problem first requires deciding which method applies, and that choice is exactly the skill exams test.
Spacing, testing and interleaving are called desirable difficulties: they slow down practice but improve long-term retention.
Sleeping after study protects new memories from interference, and a night of sleep deprivation reduces next-day learning.
A practical plan: test yourself on each lecture within a day, again after three days, and again after a week, mixing topics in each session.
In short, effortful retrieval spread over time, followed by sleep, is what turns studying into lasting memory.

tabs.title: Why cities are planting tiny forests

passages.text: Cities from Paris to Chennai are planting tiny forests, dense patches of native trees no bigger than a tennis court.
Supporters argue that these small forests cool streets and support wildlife faster than conventional parks.
The method plants three to five saplings per square meter in improved soil, so the trees compete for light and grow quickly.
A two-year study of twelve sites found surface temperatures up to 2 degrees Celsius lower than nearby paved areas.
Researchers caution that the forests need watering and weeding for the first three years, and many early plantings failed without it.
Each forest costs roughly the same as resurfacing a small parking lot, which has made them popular with neighborhood groups.
